False news can wound peace, and a world pact to fight it sits in the record as Resolution 630. The Convention on the International Right of Correction rests on a plain wish: that peoples be told the truth, in full and with trust. The pact gives a state struck by a report it holds false a right of reply. Its correction must be given the same reach, by the same channels, as the first report. The paper concludes that all such forces, including the power to shift units between areas, should sit under a single command, working closely with RAF Bomber Command. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d430:

Ambassador Hugessen received authority the night before to give Inönü the assurance he wanted, of a free discussion among equals. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d530:

frus-1944-quebec-d130:

frus-1944-quebec-d230:

frus-1945-malta-yalta-d130:

Miguel de Cervantes published Don Quixote in two parts, presented complete here in John Ormsby's classic English translation. A minor gentleman, his brains addled by chivalric romances, remakes himself as a knight-errant and rides out with the peasant Sancho Panza as squire. Windmills become giants; inns become castles; flocks become armies.

Sancho's earthy sense answers his master's glorious madness in dialogue that deepens across both parts, until each man borrows the other's nature. The 1605 novel effectively invented modern fiction and gave English the word quixotic. Ormsby's version, learned and lively, remains the traditional way in for English readers.
tob-4230:
William Gemmell's translation of the Diamond Sutra, the Chin-Kang-Ching, presents the Buddha teaching his disciple Subhuti through questions and negations. Even the highest teachings, the sutra insists, are rafts to be abandoned once the shore is reached. Form is emptiness, in the famous Mahayana formula carried through this text's tradition, and emptiness is form.

The Chinese version prized across East Asia is the form Gemmell translates, the same tradition that produced the dated printed copy of 868 AD. Short enough to read at a sitting, the text cuts at attachment to concepts, merit, and self, as its diamond title promises. Readers should expect repetition used deliberately, like a bell struck again.
tob-9047-60230:
Animals fill volume two of Bostock's Pliny, as the Natural History moves from the heavens to living things. Elephants earn Pliny's respect for their memory and near-human feeling. Lions, crocodiles, and birds follow, each with habits, habitats, and marvels attached.

Sea creatures close the survey, including monsters reported from distant waters. Pliny mixes sharp observation with travelers' tales he had no way to test, and the blend is part of the charm. Roman farmers and generals once used his notes in earnest. Modern readers get a nature program written two thousand years early, credulity and all.
tob-4130:
Volume one of Mead's Thrice-Greatest Hermes, published in 1906, lays the ground before his Hermetic translations. These prolegomena sort out the tangled history of the literature: who Hermes Trismegistus was said to be, which texts bear his name, and what world produced them.

Mead walks through late-antique Egypt and Greece, where temples, schools, and cults blended their gods and ideas. The learning is dense but humane. Readers who want the translations alone can skip ahead; students will bless the map. Checked from the 1919 edition, volume one is the learned foundation of Mead's whole Hermetic project.
way-of-a-pilgrim-french-1930:
The Way of a Pilgrim is an anonymous Russian book of the nineteenth century, first Englished by R. M. French in 1930. Its narrator is a wandering pilgrim with a lame arm, a bag of dried bread, and one burning question. He wants to learn how to pray without ceasing, as the Bible commands.

An elder teaches him the Jesus Prayer: the name of Jesus joined to the breath and the heartbeat, repeated thousands of times a day. The pilgrim walks from village to village through snow and hardship, testing the prayer as he goes. Strangers, soldiers, and peasants cross his path, and the prayer slowly changes him. The little book became the classic guide to this prayer in the West.
fortune-psychic-self-defense-1930:
Dion Fortune wrote the classic defense against occult attack in 1930. Psychic Self-Defense draws on her own cases from years of work in the field. Fortune was a trained nurse and a leading figure in British occult circles.

She tells how to spot the signs of a psychic attack and how to tell them from nerves or fraud. Then she gives the means of defense: rites, prayer, and plain steps of daily care. Her tone is calm and practical where others wrote fog. Every later book on guarding the mind against such harm cites hers.
fortune-training-and-work-of-an-initiate:
Fortune laid out the course of occult training step by step in 1930. The Training and Work of an Initiate is the mate to her Esoteric Orders, the how to that book's what. It maps the road from first study to full work in a lodge.

Meditation, symbol study, and rite craft form the spine of the course. Fortune tells what each stage does to the student and what can go wrong on the way. Her counsel is strict, sane, and shaped by her years as a teacher. The book still serves as a guide to the initiate's road.
regardie-stephensen-legend-of-aleister-c:
Two young men rose to defend Aleister Crowley when the press made him a byword in 1930. The Legend of Aleister Crowley, by Percy Stephensen and Israel Regardie, answers the scandal tales with the record. Regardie would soon serve as Crowley's secretary and student.

The book takes up the charges from the Abbey years and the drug and vice stories, point by point. It prints letters and facts meant to show a poet and thinker, not a monster. The fight over Crowley's name starts in earnest on these pages. The volume is the prime source for that fight's first round.
gould-case-for-the-sea-serpent-1930:
Rupert Gould, a naval officer of exact habits, pled the sea serpent's case in 1930. The Case for the Sea-Serpent is the most methodical brief for the beast made in its century. Gould had won fame sorting out sea mysteries and odd tales of the deep.

He answers the great Dutch treatise of Oudemans case by case, report by report. Where the proof is weak he says so; where it is strong he presses it home. His claim is plain: some sightings point to a real beast not yet in the books. Friend and foe of the serpent alike must pass through Gould.
smythe-kangchenjunga-adventure-1930:
Frank Smythe climbed on Kangchenjunga in 1929 and found marks he could not place. The Kangchenjunga Adventure, printed in 1930, tells that great expedition in full. Smythe was among the finest mountaineers of his generation, calm and exact in all things.

High on the mountain his party found footprints he reports, with care, as those of a Snow Man. A climber's plain word on such a find gave the yeti debate fresh fuel. The rest of the book is a classic of storm, height, and hard won views. Mystery and mountaineering share its pages in equal part.
scott-letters-on-demonology-and-witchcra:
Walter Scott took a cool look at witches and ghosts in Letters on Demonology and Witchcraft, his book of 1830. Scott, the great tale smith of Scotland, wrote the work as notes to a young kin. He tells famed cases of witch hunts, spooks, and deals with the dark in his rich, warm voice.

Scott doubts most of it, yet loves the tales. He blames fear, fraud, and sick minds for the bulk. His book set the tone for all cool pasts of the theme. It is a joy to read still. Scott wrote the book while his health and funds both waned. Its warmth and ease give no hint of the strain back of its birth.
tanner-narrative-of-captivity-1830:
John Tanner tells of thirty years as a captive in his Narrative of 1830, shaped by Edwin James. Snatched as a boy, Tanner grew up midst the Ojibwe round the Great Lakes. He hunts, fasts, weds, and roams their lands. His tale gives a close view of their rites, tales, and hard life in the wild north woods of that age.

Midst the lore stands the great thunder bird, whose wings make the storm's roar. Tanner heard its tale from men who held it true. The book is a chief source on that world. Its voice is plain and true.
budge-amulets-talismans-1930:
E. A. Wallis Budge, keeper of Egyptian works at the British Museum, wrote this wide survey of charms in 1930. The book was later reprinted with the title Amulets and Talismans. His ground was Egypt and the Near East, where charms had a long, rich past.

Budge sorts charms by kind, tells what each was meant to do, and gives old texts with translations. Stones, rings, and writ charms each get their place, with drawings to show their forms. It stays the classic English survey of the charm lore of the old east.
synesius-on-dreams-fitzgerald-1930:
Synesius of Cyrene was a Greek bishop and thinker of the late Roman world. Augustine Fitzgerald turned his essays and hymns into English in two parts, printed in 1930. Among the essays is his famed work on dreams, De insomniis in Latin. His hymns, writ in an old style, were prized by Greek scholars of the age.

In that essay Synesius sets out how dreams can show what is to come. He ties dreams to the soul and to a spirit that links men with the divine. The hymns show the same mind at prayer, in rich and bold Greek verse.
combe-system-phrenology-1830:
George Combe was an Edinburgh lawyer who gave his life to phrenology. His System of Phrenology came out in 1830. The book set the skull science in full, clear form. For years it served as the creed book of the whole field.

Combe lists each organ of the brain and the trait it rules. He tells how to gauge the size of each part by the skull. Tales of heads he read back up his claims in bulk. The book made head reading a mass creed of the age, taught in halls and homes.
sinclair-mental-radio-1930:
Upton Sinclair was a famed US scribe of tales with a bite. His Mental Radio came out in 1930 and took a strange turn. The book tells of tests with his wife Mary and her gift of mind sight. Albert Einstein wrote a kind word at the front of the book.

Mary would draw a sketch of a thing hid from her sight in a sealed wrap. Her hits came far too oft to be mere chance, Sinclair holds. Scores of the draws stand in print for the reader to judge. The book is the most famed first-hand tale of mind tests of its kind.
shepard-lore-of-the-unicorn-1930:
Odell Shepard wrote The Lore of the Unicorn in 1930. Shepard was a US scribe and a man of the woods and of books. The book traces one beast through tale, fact hunt, and art. No beast of myth has left so long a trail in print.

Greek and Latin scribes first tell of a fierce one-horned beast of India. The mid ages made its horn a cure for all poisons and a mark of Christ. Kings paid huge sums for horns that proved to be whale teeth. The book is the great tale of one beast in the mind of man.
thomson-history-chemistry-vol-2-1830:
Thomas Thomson was a Scots chemist and a keen hand at the tale of his science. His History of Chemistry came out in two books in 1830. Book two ends the work and takes the tale to his own day. Thomson taught chemistry at Glasgow and wrote with a clear hand.

The tale runs from the alchemists through Priestley and Lavoisier to Dalton and Davy. New gases, new metals, and the atomic scheme fill the last age. Thomson knew some of the men whose work he tells of at first hand. The set is an early full tale of the science by a man of the trade.
mathnawi-nicholson-vol-4-1930:
Book Four of Nicholson's Mathnawi came out in 1930. R. A. Nicholson's set gives Rumi's poem in Persian text with English dress. The Mathnawi is the great Sufi poem of Jalaluddin Rumi. His set of dress books is the stock one in English.

This book rounds out the pre-1931 parts of Nicholson's long work. The Mathnawi's six books of tales form a sea of Sufi lore. Each tale turns on love, loss, and the soul's hunt for God. Nicholson spent years of his life on the poem, and it shows in the care of each page.
stendhal-red-and-black-1830:
Stendhal published The Red and the Black in 1830, a French novel about ambition in the years after Napoleon. Julien Sorel is a carpenter's son with a sharp mind and big dreams. He works as a tutor, then in a great house in Paris. Love affairs with two women shape his rise and fall.

Julien plays roles to climb, yet his pride and passion betray him. A sudden act of violence ends his hopes and leads to trial. Stendhal cuts deep into the manners of church, army, and salon. The title points to the two paths open to a young man: the army's red and the church's black.
jeans-mysterious-universe-1930:
James Jeans published The Mysterious Universe in 1930, based on his Rede Lecture at Cambridge. Jeans surveys the new physics of relativity and quantum theory. He argues that the universe looks more like a great thought than a great machine. Its laws, he suggests, may be the laws of a cosmic mind.

The famous line that God appears as a pure mathematician comes from these pages. Critics praised the prose and debated the philosophy. The book sold widely and spread a sense of quantum mystery to the public. Jeans did not claim proof for his idealism. He offered it as the best reading of strange new facts.
freud-civilization-discontents-riviere-1:
Sigmund Freud published Civilization and Its Discontents in German in 1930. The English text here is Joan Riviere's translation of the same year. Freud asks why civilized life brings so much unhappiness. Culture, he argues, demands that we curb aggression and sexual drives. The curbs save us from chaos but leave guilt and malaise.

He studies religion, love, work, and the sense of guilt with bleak clarity. The death drive returns as a force behind war and cruelty. Written as Europe darkened, the book is Freud's darkest social theory. It remains his most read work of cultural criticism. Few essays on modern discontent match its reach.
weber-protestant-ethic-parsons-1930:
Max Weber's The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism appears in Talcott Parsons's translation of 1930. Weber asks why modern capitalism grew first in Protestant lands. He finds an elective affinity between Calvinist faith and the spirit of methodical work. Believers, unsure of salvation, sought signs of grace in disciplined labor and thrift.

Wealth, in this ethic, is a duty to steward, not a license for pleasure. Weber stresses that ideas and interests grow together; he does not claim faith alone caused capitalism. The essays are the most cited work in sociology. Parsons's version made Weber central to English-speaking scholarship. Debate over the thesis has run for a century.
parrington-main-currents-vol-3-1930:
Parrington died before he could fully finish his history, and the third volume came out in 1930 from his notes. It covers the years after the Civil War, when realism began to push back against polite, genteel taste. Mark Twain and other plain-spoken writers lead the story.

The volume shows authors turning toward city life, business power, and the hard facts of a changing country. Parrington praises writers who faced those facts and faults those who hid behind pretty manners. Even unfinished, the book completes one of the boldest surveys of American thought ever written.
fisher-genetical-theory-1930:
Ronald Fisher was a British statistician and biologist who set Darwin's theory on a firm math base. His 1930 book The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection joins Mendel's laws of inheritance to selection in wild populations. It is a dense book that changed its field.

Fisher shows with math how small inherited differences spread or vanish across generations. He treats topics from mimicry in moths to the balance of the sexes with the same tools. Later scholars call the book a founding text of population genetics and of the modern synthesis. He wrote for biologists, so the math comes wrapped in farm and field examples.
pickthall-meaning-glorious-koran-1930:
Marmaduke Pickthall was a British novelist who embraced Islam and spent years in India in Muslim service. His Meaning of the Glorious Koran, published in 1930, was the first Quran translation by a native English-speaking Muslim. It ranks among the two most widely used English renderings ever made.

Pickthall aimed at a plain, dignified English that echoes the Arabic without copying its form too closely. He adds short notes and a life of the Prophet by way of introduction for new readers. Muslim readers praised the version for joining sound English style to loyalty toward the source text.
avicenna-canon-medicine-gruner-1930:
Avicenna, the Persian physician and philosopher of the eleventh century, wrote the Canon of Medicine as a vast encyclopedia of healing. Gruner's 1930 English translation covers Book One of the Canon. It is the first English rendering of the medical system that ruled East and West for six centuries.

Book One lays out the theory: elements, humors, temperaments, and the causes and signs of disease. Avicenna sorts fevers, pulses, and diets with a calm, orderly mind that trusts both reason and long practice. European universities taught from the Canon into the seventeenth century, so its first book shaped doctors for ages.
suzuki-studies-lankavatara-sutra-1930:
Suzuki's Studies in the Lankavatara Sutra, published in 1930, is his landmark scholarly exposition of a dense Mahayana scripture. The Lankavatara Sutra is the text Bodhidharma is said to have handed to his successor in China. Zen counts it among its root scriptures.

The sutra teaches that the world we see is mind-only, a weaving of consciousness rather than a set of solid things. Suzuki maps its terms, compares its Chinese and Sanskrit forms, and links its thought to Zen practice. Scholars of Buddhism still treat his study as the standard guide to a hard text.
vos-pauline-eschatology-1930:
Geerhardus Vos taught at Princeton and is often called the father of Reformed biblical theology. His Pauline Eschatology, published in 1930, studies how the apostle Paul thought about the end of the age. Vos reads Paul's letters as a connected system, not as loose sayings.

He shows that Paul holds two claims together: the new age has already dawned in Christ, yet its fullness is not yet here. That already and not-yet frame, Vos argues, shapes everything Paul says about church, sacrament, and hope. Later New Testament scholars built whole schools on the structure Vos mapped here.
ockham-de-sacramento-altaris-birch-1930:
T Bruce Birch published his edition and translation of William of Ockham's De Sacramento Altaris in 1930. Ockham, the English Franciscan thinker of the 1300s, wrote the work on the sacrament of the altar, the Eucharist. Birch printed the Latin text with facing English, a critical edition.

Ockham applied his famous razor, the rule against needless entities, to questions of quantity and presence in the sacrament. His nominalism, which denied real universals, shaped the argument throughout. The edition was the only complete work of Ockham in public-domain English. Scholars of medieval philosophy use it to study both his logic and his theology of the Eucharist at first hand.
mckeon-selections-medieval-philosophers-:
Richard McKeon published Volume 2 of Selections from Medieval Philosophers in 1930, editing and translating the texts himself. The anthology runs from Roger Bacon to William of Ockham. McKeon, a scholar at the University of Chicago, built the two volumes as a gateway to medieval thought.

Writers here include Bonaventure, Aquinas, Matthew of Aquasparta, and Duns Scotus, alongside Bacon and Ockham. The Scotus selections from his Oxford Commentary and Ockham's Quodlibetal Questions were the only public-domain English versions. McKeon chose texts that show medieval thinkers arguing, not just concluding. For a generation of students, this volume was their first real meeting with scholastic philosophy in its own words.
newton-opticks-1730:
Isaac Newton's Opticks appears here in its fourth edition of 1730, the last Newton oversaw in his lifetime. First published in 1704, Opticks set out his experiments on light and color in English rather than Latin. The 1730 printing became the standard form of the work.

Newton showed that white light is a mix of colors, split by prisms and joined again by lenses. He studied thin films, diffraction, and the rings that bear his name, and pictured light as streams of tiny bodies. The closing Queries range from gravity to God's action in the world. The fourth edition preserves the founding text of physical optics as Newton finally left it.
eliot-ash-wednesday-1930:
T. S. Eliot wrote Ash Wednesday after his conversion to the Church of England in 1927. The long poem appeared in 1930 and marked a clear turn in his work. Its six parts are complete in this text.

The speaker is a man trying to leave his old life behind and learn a new faith. He renounces old loves and ambitions, climbs a winding stair, and addresses a silent lady figure. The tone is quiet, strained, and full of prayer fragments and echoes of Dante. Readers often treat the poem as Eliot's record of conversion: difficult, humble, and hard won.
hughes-not-without-laughter-1930:
Langston Hughes published Not Without Laughter in 1930, his first novel, written in his twenties with the support of a patron. Hughes grew up largely in Kansas, in towns much like the novel's Stanton. He set out to show Black American family life from inside, with its humor intact.

Sandy Rogers grows up in a house run by his grandmother, Aunt Hagar, a washerwoman of iron faith. His mother drifts, his father chases work and music, and his aunts choose opposite paths: respectability and the blues life. Tornado, school, and first jobs shape Sandy's education. Laughter, as the title insists, runs through hardship without denying it. The novel is the classic story of the Harlem Renaissance's Midwestern roots.
faulkner-as-i-lay-dying-1930:
As I Lay Dying, published in 1930, is one of William Faulkner's most famous novels. Addie Bundren, a poor Mississippi farm wife, dies after asking to be buried in Jefferson. Her husband and five children load her coffin onto a wagon and set out to honor that wish.

Fifteen voices take turns telling the story, each in short, intense sections. Flood, fire, and decay beset the journey, and each Bundren reveals private griefs and motives. Cash, Darl, Jewel, Dewey Dell, and little Vardaman all see the same events differently. Faulkner turns a grim family errand into a bold, dark, and often funny portrait of pride and endurance.
proust-sweet-cheat-gone-moncrieff-1930:
The Sweet Cheat Gone is the sixth volume of In Search of Lost Time, published in French in 1925. C. K. Scott Moncrieff translated it into English in 1930, the year of his own death. Albertine has fled the narrator's rooms, and word soon comes that she has died in a riding accident.

Grief at first floods the narrator, then slowly thins into forgetting. He tests his memories, pursues old suspicions, and finds them fading anyway. Travel to Venice with his mother brings beauty without healing. Proust shows how time erases even the sharpest pain. The volume clears the road toward the final recovery of lost time.
gide-immoralist-bussy-1930:
André Gide published The Immoralist in French in 1902, and Dorothy Bussy translated it into English in 1930. Its narrator, Michel, is a scholar who falls gravely ill on his honeymoon in North Africa. As his body recovers, his old dutiful life begins to feel like a kind of death.

Michel learns to prize health, sensation, and freedom above duty and convention. His wife Marceline sickens even as he grows strong, and he cannot turn back. Gide tells the tale in spare, lucid prose, without direct judgment. Readers must weigh Michel's liberation against its cost themselves. The short novel made Gide a central, and scandalous, figure in French letters.
svevo-confessions-of-zeno-dezoete-1930:
Italo Svevo published La coscienza di Zeno in Italian in 1923, and Beryl de Zoete Englished it in 1930 as Confessions of Zeno. Zeno Cosini, a Trieste businessman, writes his memoirs at his doctor's order as part of a cure. He promises to quit smoking on page after page, and never does.

His father, his marriage, his mistress, and his business partner all pass through his sly, self-forgiving memory. The reader learns to doubt every excuse while liking the man who makes them. James Joyce, Svevo's friend, championed the novel when Italy ignored it. The de Zoete translation was the book's first English dress. It remains a comic landmark of the modern novel.
liutprand-works-wright-1930:
Liutprand, bishop of Cremona, was a Lombard courtier and envoy whose histories sparkle with wit and spite. F. A. Wright translated his works into English in 1930. The volume holds his three surviving books: the Antapodosis, the Deeds of Otto, and his famous report of an embassy to Constantinople.

The Antapodosis, his book of payback, tells the tangled wars of Italy and the empire in his century. The embassy report of 968 mocks the Byzantine court, its pomp, its food, and its emperor, in scenes still funny after a thousand years. Liutprand gossips, flatters, and settles scores on every page. No other tenth-century writer gives so lively a picture of courts East and West.
boas-the-religion-of-the-kwakiutl-indian:
Boas spent decades recording the Kwakiutl, now known as the Kwakwaka'wakw, of British Columbia's coast. This 1930 study, drawn from dictated native texts, presents their religion as they described it themselves, in the Columbia University Contributions to Anthropology series.

The heart of the book is the winter ceremonial, the great season of dances, feasts, and secret societies. Boas explains shamanism, guardian spirits, and the rituals by which dancers took on spirit power. Because the texts came from native speakers, the work gives an insider's view rare for its time. It remains a core source on Northwest Coast religion.
lawrence-assorted-articles-1930:
Assorted Articles, published in 1930, the year of Lawrence's death, is his final collection of essays and journalism. It gathers pieces written for newspapers and magazines in his last years, on subjects from his childhood to censorship.

'Nottingham and the Mining Countryside' returns to the world of his youth and measures what industry did to it. 'The Novel' defends his art, and 'Pornography and Obscenity' attacks the censors who had hounded his work. The voice is tired, funny, and undefeated. Read as a farewell volume, it shows the range of a writer who argued with his whole age.
russell-conquest-happiness-1930:
The Conquest of Happiness, published in 1930, is Russell's practical philosophy of happiness: a self-help book by a logician, written with uncommon sense and no cant. He divides it between the causes of unhappiness and the causes of happiness.

Among the miseries he names envy, boredom, fear of opinion, and the sense of sin, each treated as a habit of mind that reason can break. The cures are equally plain: affection, work, wide interests, and effort rightly aimed. Russell writes from experience of despair in his youth. The book has comforted readers for ninety years by treating them as adults.
dewey-individualism-1930:
Individualism Old and New, published in 1930, collects Dewey's essays on the American self in a corporate age. The old individualism of the pioneer and the small owner, he argues, has lost its ground, and the modern American feels lost inside vast organizations.

Dewey refuses both nostalgia and despair. A new individualism, he says, must be built through shared inquiry, education, and democratic control of economic power. The self grows by participation, not isolation. Written at the start of the Depression, the book reads like a diagnosis still in force. It is Dewey the public philosopher at his most direct.
santayana-realm-matter-1930:
The Realm of Matter, published in 1930, is book second of Realms of Being. After the timeless essences of the first volume, Santayana turns to substance: the material world that exists, changes, and underlies every appearance.

He presents a frank materialism, honored without reduction: matter is the realm of power and fact, while spirit merely witnesses it. herschel-preliminary-discourse-1830:

plos-pone-0009530: Giant animal feeding operations worry their neighbors — but what does the science say? The paper weighs the evidence for health effects of industrial livestock farming on surrounding communities.
plos-pone-0009630: East African sleeping sickness is still diagnosed by squinting at blood under a microscope. This study screens parasite proteins to find ones that patient antibodies recognize — candidates for a simple blood test. The paper hunts the raw material for a diagnostic the field desperately needs.
plos-pone-0010430: Cells drink their surroundings through macropinocytosis, and different forms of the Abi1 protein tune the gulping. This study dissects that regulation. The paper details the control knobs on cellular drinking. The details matter for immunity, cancer, and any cell that drinks.
plos-pone-0010530: Do fish-eaters dodge depression? This cross-sectional study tests links between fish intake, omega-3s, and depressive episodes. The paper weighs the evidence for food as mood medicine. The verdict: the much-hyped fish-depression link remains unproven and murky.
plos-pone-0010630: Pancreatic cancer resists chemo — but not equally in all patients. This study identifies microRNA-21 as a marker of chemoresistance and outcome after surgery. The paper offers a test to guide treatment decisions. The marker could spare patients chemo that won't help them.
plos-pone-0010730: Clinical trials now run worldwide — but volunteers' motives differ by culture. This meta-analysis gathers qualitative studies on why Indians join trials. The paper probes motivations, trust, and ethics. The findings guide fairer trial recruitment in India and beyond. The insights protect participants everywhere.
plos-pone-0010830: The immune system might be trained to clean Alzheimer's plaques. This mouse study shows T cells aimed at amyloid plaques boost their clearance. The paper tests targeted immune therapy. The approach offers a new angle on dementia. The strategy recruits the body's own defenses.
plos-pone-0010930: Sickness drives poverty in rural Cambodia. This cross-sectional survey documents self-reported serious illnesses and their economic fallout for poor households. The paper quantifies the health-poverty trap. The data argue for stronger health safety nets. The trap keeps families from climbing out.
plos-pone-0011030: Breast tumors evolve — their proteins tell the story. This study profiles the proteome across stages of the MCF10AT breast-cancer progression model. The paper maps protein changes in tumor evolution. The finding could sharpen early detection. The map flags proteins that mark danger.
plos-pone-0011130: Mice raised in lively worlds grow stronger brains. This study tests how rich physical and social settings affect mouse movement, learning, and new brain-cell growth. The paper reveals the perks of stimulation. The finding aids brain-health science. The perks argue for richer human settings.
plos-pone-0011230: Gene-code models can mislead when guesses stand in for data. This study fixes the slant in how codon models guess their starting letter rates. The paper sharpens family-tree math. The finding improves gene history work. The sharper math better dates gene splits today.
plos-pone-0011330: Female stem cells mute one X chromosome unevenly. This study finds early female human embryonic stem cells vary in how they silence the X chromosome. The paper reveals wobbly gene control. The finding aids stem cell work. The aided work standardizes cell lines.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1230:
A second Togo cable to Sato is dated 21 July 1945. Two instructions in a day show Tokyo leaning hard on its Moscow channel. The summit in Germany was moving toward a public word on Japan, and Tokyo sensed its time shrinking.

Togo's messages balanced two needs: keep the Soviet door open, and keep Tokyo's own hard-liners from shutting the whole bid down. That balance runs through his words to Sato. This cable is one piece of it. Preserved through American codebreaking, it lets readers watch a beaten empire's last diplomacy from inside its own wires.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1330:
Britain's team tabled this proposal on 21 July 1945. It came from the end of the summit's first week, while Churchill still led the British side. The paper set London's stand on its point for the other teams to answer.

British papers of the first week carry a poignancy their writers could not feel. The government behind them was about to fall, and new men would own the stands taken here. This proposal is part of that first-week British hand. It survives in the American record, where readers can set it against the final terms and judge what the change of leaders cost or saved.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1430:
A second Soviet text dated 29 July 1945 follows in the closing run of the volume. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

The Soviet habit of tabling full drafts forced the other sides to argue on Moscow's paper or spend time writing their own. This text is part of that pressure, applied as the talks neared their end. For readers, the run of Soviet drafts is a study in negotiation by document: claims fixed in ink, defended clause by clause. What survived into the protocol can be checked line by line from these pages.
frus-1945-50-intel-d30:
General Clayton Bissell, the Army's assistant chief of staff for military intelligence, wrote to Secretary of War Patterson on 22 October 1945. Bissell spoke for the Army's own intelligence arm, G-2. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

The Army's intelligence chief had his own claims in the postwar settlement, separate from the SSU remnant housed in his department. His memorandum to the secretary shows G-2 stating its case at the top. Readers should keep the Army's threads distinct: Magruder's leftover OSS men and Bissell's uniformed service were rivals inside one building. The volume prints both sides, and the friction between them shaped what the Army finally asked for.
frus-1945-50-intel-d130:
Strategic Services Unit General Orders No. 16, dated 19 October 1946, is among the SSU's last papers in the volume. General orders announce a unit's internal acts: postings, honors, and endings. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

By October 1946 the SSU's secret operations had largely passed to the Central Intelligence Group, and the remnant was winding down. A numbered order from that season has the flavor of a colors ceremony in prose. Readers who followed the unit from Magruder's first letters will feel the thread close. The OSS's last ember was kept alive for a year by careful paper. Here it dims toward its end, as its work lives on in a new house.
frus-1945-50-intel-d230:
A memorandum from the Secretary of the Army (Royall) reached the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) on 26 November 1947. Readers meet it as document 230 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The old board and its group were gone, replaced that fall by the CIA under the new National Security Council.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d330:
On 18 November 1947, the Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Kennan) sent a memorandum to the Under Secretary of State (Lovett). It survives in print as document 330 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The old board and its group were gone, replaced that fall by the CIA under the new National Security Council.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d430:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 11, dated 6 January 1950, is document 430 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The directive opened the rule making of a new decade. By 1950 the CIA had rivals, partners, and a record of its own to defend. A fresh standing order at that point shows the Council still tuning the balance among them, three years after the agency began. The 1950 directives speak to a system that now had to manage success and strain alike. A new decade found the rule book still open, still being written by use.
frus-1861-d30:
Henry Sanford sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 18 July 1861. It is document 30 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Sanford wrote three days before the battle of Bull Run was fought in Virginia. His letter crossed the ocean in a world that did not yet know the result. That gap between event and report is the true pace of diplomacy in 1861, and this letter marks it plainly. The steamship mails set the pace of his work, each packet bringing a fresh batch of tasks. Each packet from home reset his tasks, and he worked through them in order.
frus-1861-d130:
On 12 June 1861, William Dayton reported the new French stance to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 130 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Dayton reported a Paris that had now stated its neutral course. The task shifted from shaping the stance to policing it. His mid June letter marks that turn, from the drama of decision to the grind of watching its use. Policing a neutral stance meant protests, claims, and proof, week after week. Proof, in such work, was a matter of ship names, dates, and sworn words. The turn he marks governed the file from then on.
frus-1861-d230:
In a letter dated 14 September 1861, William H. Seward gave Mr. Fogg his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 230 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d30:
In a letter dated 10 March 1862, William H. Seward gave Charles Francis Adams his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 30 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the winter of the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d130:
Seward wrote again on 18 August 1862, this time to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed as Document 130 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d230:
William Stuart wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 September 1862, in a letter printed as Document 230 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was one of two Stuart letters under that date.

Stuart wrote in the immediate wake of Bull Run, with Lee's army about to cross into Maryland. British policy turned on whether the South could prove itself a lasting nation in the field. A legation letter from this week reached London as ministers there weighed that proof. Its place in the file marks how closely diplomacy tracked the armies. Britain's first concern in Washington was the blockade and what it cost British trade.
frus-1862-d330:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, resumed the Paris mail on 3 October 1862 with a dispatch to William L. Dayton, printed as Document 330 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was one of two Seward letters to Dayton under that date in the wider file.

Early October found France ready to propose a truce jointly with Britain and Russia, waiting only for London's word. Seward's letters to Paris in this window carried the Union's refusal in advance: no foreign plan for the war would be accepted. This dispatch belongs to that firm autumn line. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d430:
On 28 June 1862 Gabriel García Tassara, Spain's minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. His note is Document 430 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Tassara had served in Washington for years and knew American politics well, which made his notes a fair test of Spanish feeling. In the summer of 1862 Spain was pulling out of the joint Mexican venture while France pressed on alone. The questions between Madrid and Washington ran from that expedition to Confederate activity near Cuba. A note like this one kept those matters in formal channels, where Seward preferred to handle them.
frus-1862-d530:
A second note of 7 June 1862 went from Roest van Limburg to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 530 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, beside its same-day companion.

Same-day pairs were common when a minister transmitted separate enclosures or took up two questions that protocol kept apart. The Dutch business of that week in Washington ran alongside the Hague correspondence of Minister Pike, and the two files illuminate each other. Van Limburg wrote as the resident voice of a small maritime power dealing with a great republic at war. His notes, formal and exact, are the Washington half of one of the volume's most complete small-country records.
frus-1862-d630:
Edward Joy Morris wrote from Constantinople to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 March 1862. His report is Document 630 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Spring 1862 found Morris reporting the Levant's quiet: American commerce moving, citizens protected, the war a subject of curiosity rather than policy at the Porte. Such reports had a negative value Washington appreciated, the assurance that one whole region required nothing. They also carried the minister's observations on the Eastern Question. That was the standing rivalry over Ottoman lands. American merchants felt it in every port from Smyrna to Beirut. The letter sustains the Turkish file's calm, expert tone.
frus-1863p1-d30:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 15 January 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 30 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Mid-January letters from Adams weighed how Britain was taking the new year of the war. The freedom edict had stirred the British public, and the legation tracked that stir with care. Adams's cool style suited the work: he reported what he saw, not what he hoped. This dispatch is a fair sample of his craft, and of the file that made his name as the Union's man in London.
frus-1863p1-d130:
London's late-March mail includes this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 26 March 1863. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 130 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Late-March mail from London came as the ship fight neared its peak. Adams reported talks, press, and the state of the yards for Washington's use. This dispatch is one of a pair sent that day. In the run of the volume it stands in one of the thickest weeks of the file. Both capitals wrote hard on the same points that week.
frus-1863p1-d230:
Reporting on 9 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is document 230 in the 1863 diplomatic papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Union wins at Gettysburg and Vicksburg in early July 1863 weakened the case for aiding the South. British leaders grew more careful, and Adams's post grew a little less tense. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d330:
Writing in Washington on 29 November 1862, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward on British business. The paper is document 330 in the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Taken as a run, these notes chart Britain slowly accepting that the Union would not collapse. That judgment, formed in Washington, helped keep Britain out of the war. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d430:
A 28 March 1863 dispatch from William H. Seward, the Secretary of State reached Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d530:
A dispatch dated 23 May 1863 went from Secretary William H. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d630:
From William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons: a letter dated 14 October 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020030:
Simon K. Cheng, Felix Olale, Ali H. Brivanlou, and their group untangled a signaling path in PLOS Biology in 2004. TGFβ signals guide how embryos grow. A protein family called EGF-CFC helps some of those signals reach their targets, and a blocker called Lefty can shut them down.

The team shows that Lefty works by jamming the EGF-CFC helpers. It stops some TGFβ signals, such as Nodal, while leaving others alone. That fine control matters in the early embryo, where signal strength sets body axes. The work explains one way embryos keep strong growth signals on a short leash, and why losing that leash can distort development.
plos-pbio-0020130:
Patrick Seale, Jeff Ishibashi, Anthony Scimè, and co-workers tested stem cells from hurt muscle in PLOS Biology in 2004. A marker protein called Pax7 is the sign of muscle stem cells. The team worked with a blood-linked stem cell group found in injured muscle and asked what Pax7 does there.

Adding Pax7 was enough to steer those cells toward becoming muscle, and without it they could not take that path. So Pax7 is both needed and sufficient for the switch, a strong claim in stem cell work. The result points to a master control for muscle fate. If that control can be used safely, it might one day help repair muscle lost to injury or disease.
plos-pbio-0020230:
Margaret J. Mackinnon and Andrew F. Read modeled a hard trade-off in malaria in PLOS Biology in 2004. Malaria parasites grow inside red blood cells, and the immune system fights them. The authors ask how that fight shapes the evolution of the parasite's virulence, meaning how sick it makes the host.

Their model suggests strong immunity can favor tougher, faster-growing parasites, since only those thrive under attack. That is a warning for vaccine design. A vaccine that cuts symptoms without blocking growth might, in theory, select for more harmful strains. The paper does not claim this has happened. It shows the risk is real enough that malaria programs should track parasite change as vaccines roll out.
plos-pbio-0020330:
Konrad P. Körding, Izumi Fukunaga, Ian S. Howard, and their team applied economics logic to movement in PLOS Biology in 2004. In economics, a utility function scores how much each outcome is worth. The authors ask whether the brain, while controlling a reach or a step, acts as if it used such a score.

By studying how people adjust to forces and errors, they infer the hidden costs the motor system seems to weigh, like effort and accuracy. If movement follows a utility rule, then many odd habits of motion fall into place. The approach also gives engineers a principled way to model human control. That helps prosthetics and robots that must move with people, not just near them.
plos-pone-0000130:
Nicholas Valmas and Paul R. Ebert published this pest control study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It compares fumigants, gases used to kill insects in stored grain, along with a phosphine booster. To run the tests safely, the authors built a new containment chamber for making concentrated phosphine gas.

Phosphine is effective but dangerous to handle, and insects keep evolving resistance to it. The authors measure how toxic the fumigants and the booster are under controlled conditions. Safer, well-measured testing helps the grain industry protect stored harvests while keeping workers safe and staying ahead of resistant pests.
plos-pone-0000230:
Bernard Le Foll, Carrie Wertheim, and Steven R. Goldberg published this addiction study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Tobacco is clearly addictive in humans. Yet experts long argued over whether nicotine by itself makes laboratory animals work to get more, as truly addictive drugs do. The authors tested nicotine's reinforcing power in non-human primates.

The title states the result: nicotine showed high reinforcing efficacy in the primates, meaning the animals worked hard to obtain it. That settles a long controversy in the authors' favor: nicotine alone can drive drug-seeking. The finding underpins tobacco regulation and the design of quitting aids.
plos-pone-0000330:
Sophie Agaugué, Laure Perrin-Cocon, Patrice André, and colleagues published this hepatitis C study in PLOS ONE in 2007. The hepatitis C virus travels in blood partly as lipo-viro-particles, virus joined with fat particles. Using particles from chronically infected patients, the authors show they interfere with TLR4 signaling in dendritic cells, damping an immune alarm pathway.

A virus that quiets the alarm can persist for decades, as hepatitis C does. The paper identifies one of its silencing tricks in real patient material. Understanding that interference helps explain chronic infection and suggests where therapies might restore the alarm.
plos-pone-0000430:
Lilian Ricaud and colleagues exposed the plant Arabidopsis to gamma rays and mapped its responses, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Gamma rays damage DNA, and plants, which cannot flee radiation, must repair or adapt. The team tracked ATM-mediated responses: ATM is a master protein that senses DNA damage and switches on defense programs, in both gene activity and development.

Arabidopsis is the standard lab plant, so its damage responses stand in for those of crops and wild plants. Knowing which genes ATM controls after irradiation helps explain how plants survive radiation in soil and seed. The work also feeds space biology, where radiation is a constant hazard for growing food.
plos-pone-0000530:
Richard P. Meisel and Stephen W. Schaeffer tracked how fruit fly chromosome arrangements pass through egg formation, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Drosophila pseudoobscura carries chromosomal arrangements, flipped segments called inversions, whose frequencies vary in nature. The team studied meiotic transmission: whether arrangements are passed on fairly or gain an edge during meiosis.

Unfair transmission, called meiotic drive, can spread a chromosome variant even if it harms the fly. Testing for drive explains otherwise puzzling patterns in wild populations. Inversions in this species are a classic system from the early days of population genetics. Modern transmission tests refine what the pioneers could only infer.
plos-pone-0000630:
Joanne Miles, Jennifer A. Mitchell, Lyubomira Chakalova and colleagues mapped gene activity around the human beta-globin locus for PLOS ONE in 2007. The locus holds the globin genes used to build hemoglobin. Strong links were already known between transcription, the copying of DNA into RNA, and chemical marks on histones, the proteins DNA wraps around.

Using a method called RNA FISH in red-blood-cell precursors, the team showed copying also runs through the stretches between genes. They tracked how that intergenic transcription and the locus's epigenetic profile change with the cell cycle and development. The picture is of a whole region switching on in a coordinated, timed way.
plos-pone-0000730:
Esmeralda A. J. M. Soares, André F. A. Santos, Thatiana M. Sousa and colleagues compared how two HIV subtypes gain drug resistance, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Subtype C is the most prevalent HIV-1 form worldwide, dominating countries with the highest HIV rates. Few studies, though, had evaluated how antiretroviral therapy performs against it. Southern Brazil was the first developing region to offer free, universal therapy.

That setting lets the authors compare resistance acquisition in subtypes B and C under real treatment programmes. If subtypes resist differently, treatment guidelines written for subtype B may fit subtype C poorly. The comparison matters most where subtype C is common and resources are thin.
plos-pone-0000830:
Anne Bergeron, Mahdi Belcaid, Grieg F. Steward and colleagues offered a divide-and-conquer plan for sequencing whole microbial communities. In environmental sequencing projects, DNA from an entire community is fragmented and sequenced, with goals including reconstructing partial or complete genomes of its members. In communities rich in species, a large fraction of the data resists assembly, because similar fragments from many species tangle together.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE method enriches the data by splitting the problem into parts it can handle. Ocean and soil samples hold most of Earth's microbes, almost none cultured. Better assembly turns raw fragments into genomes, letting science name and study organisms it cannot grow.
plos-pone-0000930:
Anna Okvist, Sofia Johansson, Alexander Kuzmin and colleagues studied a gene control system in the brains of people with alcohol dependence, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Long term drinking reshapes the brain, and those changes involve many genes at once. The NF-kappaB family of factors switches whole sets of genes on and off.

The team asked whether that system is dysregulated, thrown off balance, in chronic alcoholics. Changes there could help explain lasting cognitive problems tied to drinking. Brain tissue studies like this are hard to do and rarely direct. They still offer the closest look at what years of alcohol do inside the human brain.
plos-pone-0001030:
Satoru Yamagishi, Yoshihisa Koyama, Taiichi Katayama and colleagues built a cell model of inclusion bodies seen in inherited ALS, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In familial ALS tied to mutant SOD1, neurons and astrocytes grow hyaline inclusions, glassy clumps holding the faulty protein. How those clumps form was not known.

The team induced similar inclusions in vitro by stressing the cell's protein handling system, in cells carrying the ALS linked mutation. A lab model lets researchers test what starts clumping and what might stop it. Inclusions are a visible mark of the disease process, so a model of their birth is a useful tool.
plos-pone-0001130:
Diseases move at different speeds in a mouse and in a human, and body size is part of the reason. Jessica Cable, Brian Enquist, and Melanie Moses took up this scaling problem in a 2007 PLOS ONE article on the allometry of host-pathogen interactions. Allometry is the study of how body traits change with size.

The authors examine how body size and metabolic rate shape the pace of infection and disease progression across species. That matters for epidemiology and for a practical worry in medicine: how to translate results from small lab animals to people. A sound scaling rule makes animal studies more useful.
plos-pone-0001230:
Nigersaurus taqueti was a sauropod dinosaur that fed at ground level, cropping low plants like a lawn mower. Paul Sereno and colleagues described its skull from Early Cretaceous fossils in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The fossils document, for the first time, the cranial anatomy of a rebbachisaurid sauropod, Nigersaurus's family.

Its adaptations for ground-level herbivory are extreme: a wide, squared-off muzzle and batteries of small teeth among them. The authors argue these features challenge current ideas about feeding function and strategy among sauropods. Nigersaurus has become a textbook example of how far a plant-eating dinosaur's skull could specialize.
plos-pone-0001330:
Dental pulp from animals infected with prion diseases can carry infectivity, raising a worry for dentistry. Nadège Bourvis and colleagues assessed the risk of transmitting sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in endodontic practice, root canal work, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The concern is that the disease could spread to patients through reused instruments when prion inactivation is inadequate.

The authors model that risk in the absence of adequate prion inactivation. Prions resist standard sterilization, which makes the question more than theoretical. Their assessment helps dental regulators weigh single-use instruments and cleaning standards.
plos-pone-0001430:
Daniela Contu and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the roots of people on the island of Sardinia. The island has high rates of some immune ills, such as type 1 diabetes. Knowing its gene past is key to sound disease gene hunts there. The team read markers on the male Y chromosome across the island.

Their data point to roots that predate farming on the island. The people look gene alike in some ways, yet diverse in others. That mix shapes how gene scans should be planned there. It also adds a chapter to the tale of how island peoples formed in Europe.
plos-pone-0001530:
Xinhua Yu and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a DNA variant and multiple sclerosis. This ill harms nerve fibers, and risk runs in part through families. A variant in the DNA of the cell power units had been eyed as a risk factor. The team tested it in six European case control groups.

They report the variant does raise the risk of the disease in their data. A power unit link fits the nerve harm, since nerves hunger for energy. Each firm risk variant adds a clue to how the ill starts. It also helps sort which patients share a common root cause.
plos-pone-0001630:
Augustin Zoungrana, Boubacar Coulibaly, Ali Sié, and their co-authors ran a clinical trial in Burkina Faso on a new pairing of malaria drugs. Their 2008 PLOS ONE research article tested methylene blue combined with either artesunate or amodiaquine against uncomplicated falciparum malaria. The team looked at both safety and how well the treatment worked.

Existing drug pairs based on artemisinin are the standard cure, but safe, effective, and cheap backups are still needed as the parasite adapts. Methylene blue was the first man-made malaria drug ever used, and newer studies had hinted it could help again. The full text gives the trial design, the patient results, and the side effects seen. Trials like this tell health programs which drug pairs deserve wider use.
plos-pone-0001730:
Julia J. Day, James A. Cotton, and Timothy G. Barraclough studied how cichlid fishes multiplied in Lake Tanganyika in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Why some groups and regions hold far more species than others is a basic question in evolutionary biology. Answering it needs densely sampled family trees and good study systems. The lake's cichlids, famous for their variety, offer both.

The authors examined the tempo and mode of diversification: how fast new species arose, and whether the pace changed over time. The full text gives the family tree, the timing estimates, and the pattern of bursts or steady growth. Lake radiations like this are natural tests of how new species form, and Tanganyika is the oldest of the great African lakes.
plos-pone-0001830:
Michael L. Clawson, Juergen A. Richt, Thierry Baron, and their co-authors tested cattle genes for links to atypical mad cow disease in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Atypical bovine spongiform encephalopathies are recently recognized prion diseases of cattle. They are rare, with about 30 cases identified worldwide at the time.

prichard-masonry-dissected-1730:
Samuel Prichard, a disaffected former Mason, published Masonry Dissected in London in 1730. The pamphlet sets out the catechism of the three Craft degrees in plain question and answer. It is the first and most famous Masonic exposé, and it founded the literature of exposure that has followed the fraternity ever since.

Prichard claims to print what lodges swore their members to hide. His catechism runs through signs, words, and the story of Hiram in order. Masons denounced him, and the public bought the pamphlet eagerly. Historians still treat it as the era's best evidence for early ritual. Few exposures have been reprinted so often or believed so widely.
perjurd-free-mason-detected-1730:
The Perjur'd Free Mason Detected appeared in London in 1730, the same year as Prichard's Masonry Dissected. It answers Prichard directly. The author signs himself a Free Mason and writes in righteous anger at the betrayal of the fraternity's secrets, calling the exposer perjured for breaking his obligation.

The pamphlet is the earliest Masonic counter-pamphlet in print. It defends the Craft's honor and disputes the exposé's claims point by point. As the fraternity's first printed self-defense, it holds a pivotal place. The quarrel shows Masonry learning to fight in the new arena of cheap print. Both pamphlets together stage the birth of a very modern argument about secrecy.
